question.prompt: Claudia has \(12\) coins, each of which is a \(5\)-cent coin or a \(10\)-cent coin. There are exactly \(17\) different values that can be obtained as combinations of one or more of her coins. How many \(10\)-cent coins does Claudia have?

solutions.explanation:
Count distinct amounts by measuring them in units of \(5\) cents. Let \(t\) be the number of ten-cent coins and \(n=12-t\) the number of five-cent coins. These coins have values \(2\) and \(1\) in our chosen units.

If \(n=0\), all twelve coins are ten-cent coins, and the only positive amounts are obtained by taking \(1,2,\ldots,12\) coins. That gives only \(12\) values, so \(n\geq 1\).

For any fixed number \(j\) of ten-cent coins, where \(0\leq j\leq t\), adding anywhere from \(0\) to \(n\) five-cent coins produces all integer amounts
\[
2j,\ 2j+1,\ldots,\ 2j+n.
\]
The next such range starts at \(2j+2\). Since \(n\geq1\), this is at most one more than the preceding range's last value. Thus there are no missing integers between successive ranges. Together they give every integer from \(0\) through
\[
2t+n=12+t.
\]
No larger amount is possible, since this endpoint uses all the coins. Excluding \(0\), there are exactly \(12+t\) distinct positive values. Each value is counted once, regardless of how many coin selections produce it.

Therefore \(12+t=17\), so \(t=5\). Claudia has \(\boxed{5}\) ten-cent coins, choice \(\text{C}\).
solutions.title: Count amounts in five-cent units
